content.title: Identify the legal and regulatory requirements that actually apply to the business
content.finding: The legal and regulatory requirements that apply to the business aren't known.
content.consequence: The business currently can't say with confidence whether it's operating legally — that's not a paperwork gap, it's an unquantified risk that could surface as a fine, a forced shutdown, or a disqualifying finding at exactly the moment the business can least afford it, such as during a sale or a funding round.
content.action: Identify the specific legal and regulatory requirements that apply to this business — registration, tax, licensing, employment, data, sector-specific rules — starting with the basics: registration and tax.
content.avoid: Assuming that because the business hasn't had a problem yet, it must be compliant. Absence of enforcement so far is not evidence of compliance.
content.action_evidence: Basic requirements — registration and tax — are being met, even though other applicable requirements haven't yet been identified.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are basic requirements such as registration and tax met, with other applicable requirements not yet identified? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Identify and meet every requirement that applies, not only the basics
content.finding: Basic requirements such as registration and tax are met, but other applicable requirements — licensing, sector-specific rules, employment or data obligations — haven't been identified.
content.consequence: Meeting the obvious requirements while leaving others unidentified means the business's actual compliance position is unknown beyond the basics — a real, applicable requirement can sit undiscovered until an inspection, a complaint, or a customer's due-diligence process surfaces it.
content.action: Identify every requirement that applies to the specific activity, sector and location the business operates in, beyond registration and tax, and get each one met.
content.avoid: Relying on a generic checklist for "small businesses" instead of the requirements specific to this business's actual activity and sector. Generic compliance lists miss the sector-specific obligations that matter most.
content.action_evidence: The requirements that apply to the business have been identified, and all of them are being met.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: have the requirements that apply been identified and are they being met? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Assign responsibility for tracking compliance so deadlines and changes aren't missed
content.finding: The requirements that apply are identified and being met, but no one is specifically responsible for maintaining that — obligations aren't tracked, so a deadline or a regulatory change could be missed.
content.consequence: Compliance that's correct today but untracked tends to drift — a renewal deadline passes unnoticed, a rule changes and the business keeps operating under the old one — and the business finds out only when the consequence has already landed.
content.action: Assign responsibility for maintaining compliance to a specific person, and track obligations — deadlines, renewals, regulatory changes — so nothing is missed by default.
content.avoid: Assigning responsibility without giving that person an actual way to track deadlines and changes. A named owner with no tracking system will miss the same things an unnamed one would.
content.action_evidence: Responsibility for maintaining compliance is assigned to a specific person, with obligations tracked so deadlines and changes aren't missed.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is responsibility for compliance assigned, with obligations tracked? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Establish clarity over who owns the business and who can commit it
content.finding: Ownership, or the authority to commit the business, is unclear or disputed.
content.consequence: Unresolved ownership or authority doesn't get easier to fix with time — it gets harder, and it actively blocks things the business will eventually need: raising investment, bringing on a partner, selling, or even resolving a disagreement between the people involved.
content.action: Establish clarity over who owns the business and who has authority to commit it on the business's behalf, even before it's formally documented.
content.avoid: Leaving ownership ambiguity in place because the people involved currently get along. Goodwill isn't a substitute for clarity, and it's precisely what erodes first when a disagreement or a transition happens.
content.action_evidence: Ownership and the authority to commit the business is clear, even though it isn't yet documented.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is ownership clear, even without being documented, with no one outside the decision-maker examining significant decisions? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Document ownership and authority to commit the business
content.finding: Ownership is clear, but undocumented — and no one outside the decision-maker examines significant decisions.
content.consequence: Clarity that exists only in people's understanding isn't durable — it doesn't survive a dispute, a new investor's due diligence, or a succession event, all of which require a documented answer, not a shared understanding.
content.action: Document ownership and the authority to commit the business, in whatever form is appropriate to its size and structure.
content.avoid: Treating documentation as a formality to defer indefinitely. It only protects the business once it actually exists in writing, not once it's been discussed.
content.action_evidence: Ownership and the authority to commit the business are documented.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are ownership and the authority to commit the business documented? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Get significant decisions challenged by someone with real standing
content.finding: Ownership and authority are documented, but significant decisions receive no challenge from anyone with standing to give it.
content.consequence: A decision-maker operating without challenge is more likely to miss their own blind spots — not because of poor judgment, but because no decision-maker sees everything, and there's currently no one positioned to catch what they miss before it becomes a problem.
content.action: Get significant decisions challenged by someone with standing to give it — a co-owner, adviser, or investor — proportionate to the business's size and complexity. A sole owner can satisfy this through a standing adviser or mentor relationship with an agreed remit.
content.avoid: Seeking input only from people who are unlikely to disagree. The value of challenge comes specifically from someone willing and positioned to push back.
content.action_evidence: Significant decisions receive challenge from someone with standing to give it, proportionate to the business's size and complexity.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: do significant decisions receive challenge from someone with standing, proportionate to size? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Concentrate financial oversight explicitly with one accountable person
content.finding: There are no controls over who can spend or commit the business's money — anyone with access can commit or spend without review.
content.consequence: Without any defined limits, the business has no way to catch an error, an overcommitment, or misuse of funds before it happens — it would only be discovered after the money is already gone.
content.action: At minimum, make sure one specific, accountable person holds oversight of spending and commitments, even without formal limits yet defined.
content.avoid: Assuming that because the business is small, informal oversight by "whoever's around" is sufficient. Diffuse, undefined oversight is functionally the same as no oversight.
content.action_evidence: Control over spending and commitment now rests explicitly with one accountable person, even without defined limits yet.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does control rest entirely on one person's oversight, even with no defined limits or checks? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Define who can approve what, and up to what level
content.finding: Control rests entirely on one person's oversight, with no defined limits on who can approve what or up to what level.
content.consequence: Oversight that depends entirely on one person, without defined limits, doesn't scale and doesn't protect against that person's own errors — there's no structural line saying what does or doesn't require a closer look.
content.action: Define specific authority limits — who can approve what kinds of spending or commitments, and up to what level, even if that person is still the same one person for now.
content.avoid: Setting authority limits so high that they never actually constrain anything. The limits need to be real enough to matter.
content.action_evidence: Authority limits are defined — who can approve what, and up to what level.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are authority limits defined — who can approve what, and up to what level? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Get transactions checked by someone other than who initiated them
content.finding: Authority limits are defined, but transactions aren't checked by anyone other than the person who initiated them.
content.consequence: A limit that the same person both sets and checks against isn't an independent control — it relies entirely on that one person catching their own mistakes, which is exactly the condition under which errors and oversights go unnoticed.
content.action: Get transactions checked by someone other than the person who initiated them — an external bookkeeper, accountant, or co-owner is enough for a small business; this doesn't require employees.
content.avoid: Treating "I review my own transactions carefully" as equivalent to independent checking. The value of the control comes specifically from a second, independent perspective.
content.action_evidence: Transactions are checked by someone other than the person who initiated them, including via an external bookkeeper or accountant where the business is small.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are transactions checked by someone other than who initiated them? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Start documenting the business's most important arrangements
content.finding: Important arrangements — with customers, suppliers, employees, or partners — rest on verbal understanding.
content.consequence: A verbal arrangement gives the business nothing to point to if a customer, supplier, employee, or partner later disputes what was agreed — the business's actual position in that dispute depends entirely on whose memory of the conversation is accepted.
content.action: Start documenting the business's most important arrangements in writing, even if inconsistently at first.
content.avoid: Waiting for a dispute to happen before documenting an arrangement. By the time there's a disagreement about what was agreed, it's too late to write it down neutrally.
content.action_evidence: Some important arrangements are now documented, even though inconsistently.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are some arrangements documented, even inconsistently? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Document every important arrangement in writing
content.finding: Some arrangements are documented, but inconsistently — important arrangements still rest on verbal understanding in places.
content.consequence: Inconsistent documentation means the business is protected in some relationships and exposed in others, without a clear picture of which is which — the exposure sits exactly where it hasn't been noticed yet.
content.action: Document every important arrangement — with customers, suppliers, employees, and partners — in writing, not just the ones that happened to get written down so far.
content.avoid: Documenting only the arrangements that feel high-risk while leaving routine ones verbal. Disputes often arise in the relationships that seemed too ordinary to bother documenting.
content.action_evidence: The important arrangements are documented in writing.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are the important arrangements documented in writing? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Make documented arrangements accessible with key terms and dates known
content.finding: The important arrangements are documented, but the documents aren't held accessibly, and key terms and dates aren't known to whoever needs them.
content.consequence: A document that exists but can't easily be found, or whose key terms no one currently remembers, provides little more protection than no document at all when a question about it actually comes up.
content.action: Hold documented arrangements accessibly, and make sure key terms and dates are known to whoever needs them — not filed away and forgotten.
content.avoid: Treating "it's saved somewhere" as equivalent to accessible. If finding it and knowing its terms takes a search, it isn't yet doing its job.
content.action_evidence: Documents are held accessibly, with key terms and dates known to whoever needs them.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are documents held accessibly, with key terms and dates known to whoever needs them? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.
